newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ MAY EXEMPT OVER 60S FROM COMPULSORY PENSION.
newsitem.headline: NZ MAY EXEMPT OVER 60S FROM COMPULSORY PENSION.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters said on Friday that if New Zealand goes ahead with its proposed compulsory superannuation scheme people aged 60 and over on the start-up date might be exempted from contributing to the scheme. In the prepared text of a speech he was due to deliver to a South Island financial advisors meeting, Peters said Treasury's design team for the proposed Retirement Savings Scheme (RSS) was "considering an exemption, for those people who reach retirement age during the first five years after the RSS begins".
"That means that those people age 60 and over on the start-up date for the new scheme will be exempted from contributing," he explained.
Peters, who is also Deputy Prime Minister, implied that the idea was linked to addressing concerns about the transitional phase of any new system among people approaching retirement.

As has already been announced, people above retiring age will receive the full amount of pension entitlement under the current New Zealand Superannuation scheme, and in all Peters envisages a 40-year "gradual and phased changeover period".
Full details of the proposed RSS scheme will only be released in July, leaving the government just a few weeks to prepare voters for a referendum on the issue due in September.

A vote on RSS was a central policy plank of the New Zealand First party, led by Peters, when it entered government last year and commentators see it as a crucial personal crusade for Peters, now flagging with his party in the popularity stakes.
Peters took issue with some of the opinion polls that have already been done on RSS, noting that people were being canvassed for their views on a scheme whose design has not yet been released.

"Some commentators have been trying to sink the RSS before the design has even been unveiled...," he said, adding that taking the results of speculative polls and announcing that the referendum is set to be lost "is a nonsense".
However, he found some useful aspects in the detail of one survey which assessed how different sectors of the community viewed the notion of savings-based retirment income scheme.

"Those who are opposed to savings-based supperannuation seem to be older, while those who support such a scheme are predominantly younger," he observed, refering to a poll by fund managers and life insurers Colonial detailed earlier this week.
"Those who are retired have nothing to fear from the RSS. Indeed, RSS is the only safeguard to preserve what they have now," Peters argued.
As for younger people, he said he believed they understood "this may be their one chance to get the non-savers off their back once and for all."
Peters used much of his address to once more drive home his belief that taxes will inevitably rise if RSS is not pursued.
"Keeping our present system of superannuation means any one of the following -
* tax increases in the forseeable future,
* or drastic expenditure cuts across the board, including for necessary services such as health and education,
* or drastic cuts to the current rate of superannuation,
* or increased government debt,
* or an increase in the eligibility age for superannuation,
* or a combination of all of these."
"There is no other way to sustain a system like our currrent universal superannuation scheme. That is what happened these last 20 years and nothing will stop this trend."

"Whatever else you may believe to have heard about superannuation over the past few months, and however you decide to vote in the referendum, you must do so with the knowlege that in order to carry on as we are today, your taxes WILL go up."
--Andrew Huddart, Wellington newsroom +64 4 471 4273
